Water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) is an invasive aquatic plant with rapid growth doubling every 5–15 days under optimal conditions.
WH biochar was produced by pyrolyzing dried WH powder at 400, 500, and 600 °C under nitrogen atmosphere.
The WHBC-PVA composite disks were fabricated by mixing 16 g biochar with 100 cm3 of 10% w/v PVA solution, then dried at 110 °C for 24 hours.
The composite disks measured 9 cm in diameter and 0.5 cm in thickness for sound absorption testing.
BET surface area of WHBC600-PVA was the highest at 27,378 m2/g, with specific surface area of 335,514 m2/g.
WHBC500-PVA had a surface area of 18,575 m2/g but showed the best sound absorption performance.
Pore volumes increased with pyrolysis temperature: 0.033 cm3/g (400 °C), 0.035 cm3/g (500 °C), and 0.045 cm3/g (600 °C) by adsorption analysis.
Sound absorption coefficient (SAC) of WHBC500-PVA reached 21.03% (0.2103), higher than WHBC400-PVA (9.08%) and WHBC600-PVA (6.94%).
Styrofoam used as control had a SAC of 4.37% (0.0437) under the same test conditions.
Sound absorption was measured at 440 Hz frequency with initial sound intensity of 84 dB.
The impedance tube used was 95 cm long with inner diameter 9.5 cm and outer diameter 9.8 cm.
Nitrogen adsorption–desorption isotherms indicated the presence of mesopores (2–50 nm) with cylindrical shape in the composites.
FTIR spectra confirmed functional groups from cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and bonding interactions between WH biochar and PVA.
SEM imaging showed no significant visual differences among composites pyrolyzed at different temperatures.
Nitrogen condensation in pores during BET analysis accounted for about 6–7% of pore volume, indicating capillary condensation in mesopores.
The optimal pyrolysis temperature (500 °C) likely promoted the strongest chemical bonding between WH biochar and PVA.
The porous structure and chemical bonding contribute synergistically to sound absorption by dissipating sound energy.
The WHBC-PVA composite is the first reported use of water hyacinth biochar-based composite as a sound absorber.
The composite fabrication process is simple, low-cost, and environmentally friendly.
The study highlights the potential of utilizing invasive water hyacinth biomass for sustainable acoustic materials.
